director.chapterArc: Survivalist journey from physical exertion toward existential crisis; arc moves from counting supplies to discovering a resonant power linked to the fever.
director.restraintNote: Maintain clinical precision and emotional distance throughout. Avoid melodrama in pain or fear scenes; let physical sensations carry the weight.

cues.delivery: Measured counting establishes stakes. Jab's internal arithmetic is rhythmic and functional.
cues.from: The twists of bark were folded in birch paper the way the Elder folded them, and there were nineteen.
cues.through: Jab counted them by touch, because striking a light would have woken Tonk, and Tonk had been asleep for less than an hour. Nineteen. Two a day was the schedule. The road had six days left in it if the weather held and eight if it did not, and nineteen halved came to nine and a half, which was more than eight. He had margin. The only reason a person counted margin at the cold end of a night was that he was about to spend some of it.
cues.reason: Establishes the hyper-vigilant narrator stance bound to Jab's sensory experience.

cues.delivery: Jab speaks with low-register reassurance. No condescension; he treats Tonk as a partner.
cues.through: He took one twist out and folded the paper back over the others and put them in the inside pocket, and then he sat in the dark with the twist in his fist and did the arithmetic one more time, because it was not only a twist. The night dose belonged four hours from now. Spending it now meant the morning dose came late, and the morning was the long climb out of the draw, and a late dose meant carrying Tonk up eight hundred feet of switchback through the worst hour the bark could give him.
cues.reason: Differentiates Jab's dialogue from the narrator through rhythm and vocabulary.

cues.delivery: Tonk speaks breathily and slurred by fever. Rhythm is erratic with pauses.
cues.from: "Bark," Tonk said, from a long way down.
cues.reason: Character differentiation: Tonk's voice is physically strained.

cues.delivery: Clinical observation of the fever arc. Jab monitors pulse with detached focus.
cues.from: He held his fingers against the side of Tonk's throat until the fast little pulse under them began, slowly, to slow. The fever was up but not at the top of its arc — he had learned the difference in the first week, the way the skin went from hot-and-damp to hot-and-dry, and this was the damp kind, which was the better kind. He laid his brother back down on the folded hide and tucked the blanket under him and left the bad leg out from under it the way it had to be.
cues.through: Then he sat with his back against the lattice of the frame and did not sleep, because it was two hours to light and sleeping for two hours was worse than not sleeping at all.
cues.reason: Narrator returns to neutral observer stance after dialogue.

cues.delivery: Tactile description of the frame. Rhythmic cadence mimics Jab's expertise.
cues.from: He broke camp in the gray. It had a fixed order now, and the order was the only thing standing between him and the kind of mistake that ended people out here: fire drowned and scattered; water skins filled and both stoppered, because he had lost half a skin on the third day to one that was not; food bag closed with the double turn; blanket rolled inside the hide so the hide took the wet. Then the frame.
cues.through: The rail was why he could not walk through a gap narrower than his own shoulders and a hand more. The belt was why he could not get out of the thing with one hand. Both of those were the price of Tonk not screaming, and Jab had paid it nine days running and would go on paying it.
cues.reason: Technical exposition integrated into sensory experience.

cues.delivery: Brief exchange. Jab's voice is measured; Tonk's is sleepy and factual.
cues.through: "Asleep people talk," Tonk said, with his eyes shut and his mouth doing something that was very nearly a grin, and Jab, who had slept perhaps four hours in three days, found that he had laughed.

cues.delivery: Loading sequence. Jab's internal monologue is functional; Tonk's dialogue is sharp.
cues.from: Loading took a long time and could not be hurried. He put his hands under and lifted with the bad leg supported all the way along its length, elbow under the knee, forearm under the calf, the way the Elder had shown him with her hands on his hands, and Tonk still made a sound at the turn no matter how slowly it was done. Then the seat, then the ankle strap, then the thigh strap, then the chest band, then the blanket, then the hide over the top, then the wooden fish put into Tonk's hand because if the fish was not in his hand before the hood went up there would be a search, and a search meant unloading.
cues.through: Tonk considered this with the seriousness of a man weighing a season's fish. "He'll see," he decided.

cues.delivery: Physical exertion described with restraint. Jab's pain is noted but not dramatized.
cues.from: Jab backed into the frame, got the belt around his hips and cinched it on the fourth hole, which had been the third hole nine days ago, and stood up out of his knees with a hundred and some pounds of brother and food and hide and water coming up with him.
cues.reason: Narrator remains bound to Jab's sensory input.

cues.delivery: Counting rests establishes the high-country rhythm.
cues.from: The climb out of the draw took two hours and ten rests.
cues.reason: Establishes the 'walking pace' of Jab's internal monologue.

cues.delivery: Dialogue about the rock. Tonk's observation is factual; Jab's response is accepting.
The slip. Pacing shifts from slow deliberation to immediate reaction.
cues.from: They did not come back. There was nothing to come back to, and Tonk knew that in the way a four-year-old knew it, which was that he knew it on some days and on other days he did not, and there was no telling in advance which kind of day it would be. Jab had learned to let it stand. Correcting him took nothing away from him and cost them both an hour.
cues.through: Jab put his forehead against the rock and laughed, and it came out shaky. His arms had begun the fine shudder they did afterward. He stayed where he was until it stopped, because this was the tenth time in nine days that something like that had happened, and he had made himself a rule about it after the second: never take the next step angry. The next step was the one that mattered. The one behind him was finished.
cues.reason: Sharp pacing shift required for physical failure.

cues.delivery: The jay story. Jab's voice is dry; Tonk's reaction shows the fever's effect.
cues.from: They made the top at the tenth rest, and he had been right about ten, and he took no pleasure in it.
cues.through: Jab said what the jay said, twice, badly enough that the actual jay took offense and left, and Tonk laughed until he coughed, and the cough turned into a small sound at the end of it as the coughing moved the leg, and the laughing stopped.
cues.reason: Levity highlights tragedy rather than relieving it.

cues.delivery: Medical inspection. Jab's observation is cold and clean; no grief expressed.
cues.from: They took the noon rest on a windfall with a view down the length of the valley they had come up.
cues.through: Which was true, and which was also the medicine wearing off, and which was also, Jab had come to suspect, not the whole story — because the big one had begun to come at other times lately, in the middle of good afternoons, out of nothing. He filed that too.

cues.delivery: Feeding and singing. Jab's voice is economical; Tonk's demand for the song shows his need.
cues.from: He fed them both. Half a smoked fish each and a piece of root that had to be chewed for a long time before it agreed to be food. Thirteen fish. Tonk ate all of his, which was the best news of the day, and asked for more, which was the second-best, and Jab gave him a second half out of tomorrow and told himself he would set snares tonight.
cues.through: "I'm not," Jab agreed, and sang the four, and Tonk corrected him twice on words he was fairly sure he had right, and Jab let him have both.

cues.delivery: Decision to move. Jab's internal logic is clear and urgent.
cues.from: The rain came at the middle of the afternoon.
cues.through: Wet camp meant Tonk wet. Tonk wet meant Tonk cold. Tonk cold, with the fever running its arc, was the thing the Elder had spent the longest on and had come back to twice, and that was how Jab knew which part of her instructions she had actually been frightened about.

cues.delivery: Rain sequence. Jab's voice is protective; Tonk's fear is direct.
Discovery of power. Jab's realization is quiet and unsettling.
cues.from: The creek country came up out of the rain at him in pieces — a sound first, a big unbroken roar down and to the left that he did not like the size of, then alder, then the dark of the fir stand exactly where the Elder had put it, and he went into the trees and out of the wind and stood still for a moment in the sudden quiet with water running off his chin.
cues.through: Then he put more wood on the fire, and reset his hand where it had been, and made himself stay awake for the hour that the fever would take to turn, because whatever else was true, that hour was coming and somebody had to be in it with him.
cues.reason: Narrator returns to neutral observer as the scene resolves.

pauses.after: He got his left hand into the rock. There was nothing in the rock to get a hand into — no crack, no ledge — so what he actually did was press his whole forearm flat against the cliff and pull himself into it the way you pull a door shut, and the frame swung back, and Tonk shrieked once, short, more startled than hurt, and then they were standing still on a foot and a half of turf with Jab's cheek against cold stone.
pauses.reason: Scene break after the slip; pause for physical realization of danger.

pauses.reason: Speaker reset after the flashback to the Kindling; transition back to present sensation.
Isolating the crucial distinction in Jab's realization about the power source.
